title: MetaphIR: Corpus-Scale Applicability Analysis for LLVM Peephole Optimizations
summary:
Peephole optimizations replace short source instruction sequences with more efficient equivalents, typically guarded by preconditions such as requiring a constant operand to be a power of two. Since every new rewrite adds maintenance burden and compile-time cost, compiler developers need to know how often real-world programs both match the source pattern and satisfy its preconditions before committing to an implementation. Existing workflows fall short: structural search over an intermediate representation (IR) corpus of 4.8 million functions ignores preconditions and therefore overcounts, whereas implementing the rewrite and recompiling the corpus yields exact counts only after paying the engineering cost, with each run of the corpus's on-demand recompilation pipeline taking a median of 47 minutes. This delay is especially limiting when generalizing a rewrite, as developers often iterate over multiple variants to trade off coverage against complexity.
  We introduce MetaphIR, a system pairing a domain-specific language for expressing LLVM peephole optimizations with an indexed search engine over large IR corpora. Using a syntax modeled on LLVM's C++ matchers, MetaphIR patterns augment LLVM IR with holes and Boolean preconditions over matched values. To answer queries at interactive speed, MetaphIR builds compact per-function summaries ahead of time and uses abstract interpretation over those summaries to soundly filter out functions that cannot satisfy a query's constraints. Across twenty recent peephole optimizations from LLVM's InstCombine pass, MetaphIR recovers the exact set of functions where each rewrite applies in isolation, achieving 100% precision and recall. Queries complete in a median of 1.27 seconds---a 22x speedup over a full corpus scan---enabling developers to quickly gauge an optimization's reach and generality prior to implementation.

title: Detecting Empty Abstractions and Pruning Dead Paths in the Linux eBPF Verifier with Abstract Step Functions
comment: 23 pages
summary:
The Linux kernel's eBPF verifier uses abstract interpretation to ensure the safety of user-provided programs before execution. It tracks each register with multiple interval domains and a bitwise domain (tristate numbers). Refining the abstract state at conditional branches can produce mutually contradictory constraints across domains, indicating an unreachable path. However, the verifier lacks an empty-set ($\bot$) representation and cannot detect when these domains have an empty intersection, causing it to analyze dead paths. Passing such contradictory states into domain reduction or downstream operators violates their implicit non-emptiness precondition, triggering domain invariant violations. This has been a multi-year issue in the Linux kernel causing production outages, false rejections, and state explosion.
  This paper presents a sound and complete constant-time emptiness check across the eBPF verifier's abstract domains to prune dead branches. We introduce abstract step functions, a general framework that tests whether intervals and non-convex domains intersect in O(1) time without scanning individual values. We develop tnum_step, a formally verified constant-time operator that jumps to the next integer satisfying a tristate bitmask. Using tnum_step, we design a multi-domain emptiness check that detects contradictory states during branch refinement and immediately prunes unreachable branches, eliminating the root cause of dead-branch invariant violations. Our technique prevents invariant violations, state explosion, and false rejections while incurring negligible (1.48%) overhead across Linux kernel selftests and production suites such as Cilium. Our tnum_step operator has been upstreamed into the mainline Linux kernel.

title: Validating Concurrent Correctness Witnesses with Ghosts by Thread-Modular Abstract Interpretation
comment: Accepted to POPL '27; Extended version with appendices
summary: Concurrent programs are notoriously difficult to write and to reason about, and even tools based on sound theoretical foundations can produce incorrect results due to implementation bugs. Correctness witnesses have been proposed as a way to increase the confidence in the verdicts of software verifiers by enabling independent validation. Recently, correctness witnesses have been extended to the concurrent setting, by introducing ghost variables to allow encoding more expressive invariants. While different approaches to producing witnesses with ghosts exist, validation techniques are still lacking; instead of leveraging the information encoded in the ghosts to guide the validation process, validators merely treat ghost instrumentation and invariants over ghost variables as additional proof obligations. We propose a novel framework for the validation of concurrent correctness witnesses that exploits the semantic information encoded in ghost variables. It combines a checking phase, which establishes the semantic content of the ghost instrumentation, with an exploitation phase making use of this information. Both phases are formulated as thread-modular abstract interpretation. In particular, we consider two different classes of ghost variables and techniques for exploiting them, one based on resource invariants and one based on phases. Phase ghosts guide the degree to which the abstract interpretation considers interleavings instead of always abstracting them coarsely. In this way, the abstract interpreter can validate witnesses containing invariants beyond the reach of unguided thread-modular analysis, while still retaining its scalability benefits. We have implemented our framework in a static analyzer and evaluate it on witnesses encoding resource invariants obtained from a state-of-the-art software verifier, as well as on hand-crafted witnesses encoding phase information.

title: A Principled Approach to Concurrency, Nondeterminism, and Asynchrony in Choreographies
comment: 31 pages including appendix
summary:
Choreographic programming (CP) describes a distributed system as a global program and compiles it into communicating network programs via endpoint projection (EPP). Asynchrony captures the independent progress of communicating processes, while nondeterminism captures the range of behaviours that can arise from their interactions. However, the integration of both features into a theory of CP is absent.
  We present Nyarlathotep, the first asynchronous nondeterministic CP framework. We define its operational semantics of choreographies and networks using labelled transition systems. Besides asynchrony and choreographic nondeterminism, Nyarlathotep supports expressive features including general branching, out-of-order execution, and general recursion with parameterised procedures that processes can enter independently. We prove EPP sound and complete, establishing strong behavioural equivalence between the semantics of choreographies and their projected networks. We prove that projected networks are communication-safe and deadlock-free. We mechanised all our results in Lean 4.

title: A Metric for Semantic Graph Matching of No-Code Workflows
comment: 18 pages, 6 figures, 11 tables, including appendices
summary: No-code and agentic systems increasingly produce executable workflows, but workflows cannot be compared adequately as strings because typed operations, parameters, and directed connections jointly determine the artifact. We define a semantic graph-matching distance for finite attributed workflow graphs. A partial one-to-one node matching determines node-substitution and directed labelled-edge disagreement, while unmatched nodes incur a positive null cost. Under a fixed type hierarchy, encoder, field universe, and metric-compatible primitive distances, the objective is a metric on workflow graphs up to attributed isomorphism. A padded Hungarian procedure provides a scalable feasible upper bound distinct from the exact objective. We evaluate the metric on 4,705 public n8n exports, representing 2,282 distinct normalized-graph hashes, 73,057 nodes, and 469 observed node types. Across 32,093 branch-and-bound-complete evaluations, the mean raw distance is near zero under surface-preserving transformations ($1.21 \times 10^{-5}$) and rises to $0.584$ under major type or subgraph changes. On a complete 796-hash panel, accumulated edit count has Spearman $ρ= 0.520$ with distance, while the median within-workflow correlation is $0.975$. One- and three-perturbation systems have marginal means of $0.307$ and $0.763$, and all 117,312 evaluated triangle orientations have non-negative slack. Weight ablations preserve the positive edit-count association across tested configurations. These tests support numerical consistency, near-invariance to surface-preserving transformations, graded sensitivity to semantic and structural change, and robust discrimination across controlled modifications. The metric measures artifacts and does not by itself assert behavioural equivalence under external state or runtime data.

title: The Obsolescence of High-Level Code: Agentic Generation from Semantic Artifacts
summary:
This paper argues that high-level source code need not remain the primary persistent artifact of software development when AI agents can generate, validate, and regenerate executable implementations from semantic intent. We place this claim in historical context by revisiting application generators, CASE tools, model-driven development, and platforms such as GeneXus, where developers already maintained higher-level representations from which code and other artifacts were derived.
  We propose a unifying view in which generation is the fundamental operation: given a semantic specification S = (R, C, I, T, O), maintained as the semantic authority, an agent produces a generated executable artifact A. Functional requirements, contracts, and interfaces are assessed as semantic obligations, while tests and operational objectives are assessed by an explicit external oracle V(A, S). We operationalize this framework through an experiment in independent generation: multiple LLVM artifacts are generated directly from one frozen semantic authority and evaluated by the same external oracle.
  The experiment reports regeneration coherence on an evaluated domain, not a proof of absolute correctness. It provides initial evidence that independently generated executable artifacts can produce the same observable outcomes under a common semantic authority and external oracle. We conclude by discussing reproducibility, specification-centered evolution, and the implications of treating implementation representation as a deployment choice rather than the primary maintained artifact.

title: Tracing the Messy Middle: A Runtime Transaction Schema for AI Coding Agents
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Peer-reviewed; accepted for presentation at the KDD 2026 Workshop on Agentic Software Engineering (SE 3.0), August 10, 2026, Jeju, Korea
summary:
AI coding agents are increasingly integrated into software development, yet the field lacks a systematic feedback loop to improve their behavior in practice. Artifact datasets capture final outputs such as code patches, commits, and benchmark outcomes, but omit the messy middle of the development lifecycle: the failed retries, fallback strategies, routing decisions, and abandoned sessions that determine operational cost, reliability, and productivity.
  We propose an observability framework that captures these runtime behaviors as structured transaction records, enabling engineering coaching grounded in behavioral evidence, workflow optimization at the stages where tasks break down, and routing policy iteration measured by total task cost rather than per-request price. We define the runtime transaction schema this architecture requires and demonstrate initial feasibility through Agent Token Manager (Atm), a local-first prototype that reconciles gateway records and transcript evidence without exposing prompt content to external collectors. Finally, we identify three open research problems that must be solved to scale these feedback mechanisms: trace reconciliation without shared request identifiers, outcome linking across asynchronous systems, and intervention causality. Treating the linkage between sessions and artifacts as a fundamental infrastructure requirement provides a structured foundation for understanding and optimizing agent behavior.

title: f2x50: A Repository-Scale Benchmark for Fortran-to-X Software Migration
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Repository-level migration requires more than translating isolated functions: it must preserve behaviour across modules, shared state, build structure, and dependencies. Existing translation benchmarks predominantly cover small programs or small repositories, or fixed and widely studied language pairs. We present f2x50, a target-independent benchmark comprising 50 public Fortran repositories pinned to exact Git revisions. It contains 12,116 Git-tracked Fortran files and 6,569,806 lines, divided into three structural-complexity tiers and paired with 561 deterministic behavioural probes. Of these probes, 446 compile pinned source files with small drivers and span 131 repository--routine pairs. Every repository has at least five direct checks that collectively execute at least two routines. f2x50 provides target-independent tools for acquisition, validation, licence review, and reproducibility, together with a reference adapter for evaluating Python targets. The remaining probes are explicitly classified as extractions, inline reimplementations, or synthetic fixtures. The benchmark therefore supports comparable evaluations across migration tools and target languages.

title: ETA: Exit on Tool Arrival in Speculative Agent Loops
comment: 12 pages
summary: Tool-using language agents in explicit thinking modes generate long chains of thought before acting, making each turn inherently serial: later tokens depend on the tool observation. Recent speculative tool dispatch methods overlap tool execution with reasoning, but offers limited benefit when reasoning dominates latency. We present ETA, that treats the speculative fork not as an actuator but as a sensor of the model's decision state, using it to terminate the reasoning of the main decode. It truncates reasoning only when the prediction is stable, agrees with the dispatched call, passes a free probe measuring whether a call will be emitted at all, and the tool result has arrived: a deadline that bounds per-turn regret by the remaining decode cost. ETA achieves speedups of 1.33x on tau2 airline/retail, 1.26x on tau2 telecom, and 1.13x on BFCL v4 multi-turn. On tau2, it decodes 24% fewer tokens at a nearly unchanged per-token rate without dropping action quality.

title: Agent-Native Applications: A New Application Paradigm
comment: 21 pages, 8 figures, 1 table, 1 code listing; published in IEEE Access
summary: Traditional application architectures assume behavioral logic authored in advance, leaving reachable behavior largely bounded by explicit code and workflow rules. Large language model (LLM)-based agents challenge this assumption by enabling runtime reasoning and autonomous action to become part of application behavior, allowing applications to address situations not enumerated at design time. Extending this pattern, this paper identifies a new application paradigm in which LLM-based agents serve as central reasoning and action components responsible for the application's core logic and, where permitted, for adapting the application graph itself at runtime. We call these agent-native applications. While such applications significantly expand their possible behavioral space beyond explicit code and workflow rules, they also face a major control problem in which useful agentic reasoning should be preserved while application behavior should remain within a permissible space. We therefore propose an architectural model that represents the application as a portable graph of agents, tools, data sources, and human-in-the-loop (HITL) checkpoints, and encodes the application's permitted behavior as a behavioral envelope within a declarative application specification. At runtime, an application orchestrator serves as the control plane that coordinates tasks and governs how the graph and its permissions evolve, while an agent mesh serves as the data plane that mediates policy-relevant interactions and produces audit events. We then discuss the trust layer that makes agent-native applications governable and the supporting foundations required for practical operation. Two use cases illustrate the architecture, while Agent-Native Runtime (ANR) demonstrates selected core mechanisms in an executable prototype.

title: What Moves the Ceiling on Automated Audit: from General Code to Scientific Code, Results and Data
comment: 27 pages, 4 figures, 1 table
summary: Models increasingly check what other models write. We study one shipped arrangement, in which an auditor from a different vendor reads the work and deterministic checks verify what code can verify, and measure its limits against ground truth no model supplies. On general-purpose code with hidden tests, eight readings of the auditor reach 30.0% recall [20.0, 40.7] at 16.0% [10.1, 22.3] flags on correct code, with diminishing returns and no plateau. The reading model (confounded with its sampling), one rulebook sentence and the decision rule each move that figure, and much of what is missed is, on a post hoc rating, behaviour the specification never determined. In three preregistered science studies, checking that reported numbers trace to their sources flagged all 49 inconsistent reports and none of 25 consistent fabrications, of which the model auditor flagged 23 (21 with a sound finding, post hoc); on data, a documentation-derived validator and the auditor flagged overlapping but different faulty items, together 112 of 140 at a 2.9% [0.7, 5.7] flag rate on clean data; and on scientific code, reframing the task around one step cut flags on correct code from 68.7% to 36.0%. Where both tiers ran, the deterministic one flagged no clean item and could not see consistent error; the model saw some and erred itself. Studies making model calls were preregistered, the two unregistered analyses are named, and every quoted report passed independent cross-vendor review.

title: Who Changed the AI Agent's Rules? Measuring How AI Coding Agents Escalate Authority in CI/CD Pipelines
comment: Accepted for publication at the Research track of PROFES (Product Oriented Software Process Improvement) 2026 conference, Karlskrona, Sweden
summary:
AI coding agents can modify CI/CD control-plane structures, including workflows and permission settings, thereby extending their authority beyond routine code changes. Because such modifications can affect an entire development pipeline, this study examines the trade-off between execution cost and governance risk in agentic CI/CD. We introduce a joint penalty model, P(M), that combines these two dimensions and evaluate it on all 932,791 agent-authored pull requests in the AIDev dataset, covering five autonomous coding agents. Each pull request is automatically classified by authority scope - data-plane or control-plane - and assigned a penalty score.
  We found that control-plane actions have a 2.3x higher mean joint penalty than data-plane actions (0.498 vs. 0.218) and a 3.9x higher mean governance risk (0.530 vs. 0.135), which means that they indeed increase the risk. All 775 pull requests in the extreme-risk category, defined as P(M) > 0.8, modify the control plane. Policy-violation flags occur in 46.6% of all control-plane pull requests and in 63.6% of merged control-plane pull requests. We have also found an indication that governance risk differs substantially across agent implementations, ranging from 0.166 for Cursor to 0.328 for Copilot in mean joint penalty. These differences are not explained by execution cost or merge rate, suggesting that authority policies should be calibrated for individual agents. Manual assessment of 34 pull requests yielded a Cohen's kappa of 0.72 for the authority-scope classifier.
  The results show that a single compound metric can identify and measure changes to CI/CD governance structures at scale. The proposed framework supports detecting high-risk pull requests and comparing governance behavior across agent implementations, providing a basis for authority tuning and pipeline governance in agentic software development.

title: From Data Quality to Data Trustworthiness in AI-Driven Software-Intensive Embedded Systems: A Systematic Review
comment: This is a preprint version and the final version will appear in the proceedings of PROFES 2026
summary: AI-driven software-intensive embedded systems (SIES) depend on data during development and operation. Poor data quality (DQ) may weaken data trustworthiness, yet evidence about its effects and lifecycle management remains fragmented. This systematic literature review synthesizes 27 primary studies published from January 2020 to February 2026. It examines DQ concerns and evidence linking them to reduced data trustworthiness, along with assessment and management methods. The review identifies 16 concerns organized as Source Quality and Content Quality. Studies provide DQ-based scores and evidence of effects on model or decision performance. Synthesis suggests upstream source or handling problems may become embedded in training baselines and remain difficult to detect at runtime. Eight method categories were identified. Runtime monitoring is the largest category, while upstream and training-time controls remain poorly integrated with runtime assurance. No study covers the full lifecycle. Data trustworthiness supports reliable SIES decisions but is one component of AI-system trustworthiness.

title: Measuring What Matters in the Age of AI: The Research Software Metrics Landscape
summary: Research software now serves as a primary instrument of science, but the methods the community uses to judge its quality, sustainability, reuse, and impact remain scattered across software engineering, open science, FAIR software, citation, and research-assessment literature. AI-assisted development sharpens the problem: code can be produced at rates that outpace human review capacity, provenance and attribution are harder to track, scholarly credit systems cannot keep pace, and existing metrics inherit assumptions about how research software gets developed that may no longer apply. To aid in navigating these challenges, we present a focused landscape synthesis of research software metrics based on 49 substantive references, organizing the recurring metrics into eight families described by data source, claimed construct, evidence of validity, automation potential, and susceptibility to misuse. Many widely cited research software metrics serve as partial signals but make weak standalone measures of scientific impact. The AI era opens or widens gaps around provenance, maintainability of generated code, reviewer effort, model and data dependencies, reuse and community-health signal inflation, and credit for human labor that AI does not perform. We argue for responsible, contextual, mixed-method use of research software metrics, and offer decision guidance for Research Software Engineers (RSEs), principal investigators, institutions, and funders selecting metrics that support better software, fairer credit, and more trustworthy science. All findings rest on the 49-reference focused review; a reproducible search-and-triage protocol and a 727-record triaged corpus accompany the paper as a transparency artifact for a future full systematic mapping study.

title: Structure-Behavior Coalescence: A Definition of Systems
summary: For more than seventy years, systems engineering has developed extensive models and frameworks, yet the fundamental question of what constitutes a system remains insufficiently formalized. Existing approaches often treat structure and behavior as separate aspects, leaving their unity, system identity, and consistency conditions insufficiently defined. This paper introduces Structure-Behavior Coalescence (SBC) as a formal framework that defines a system as an integrated entity in which structure and behavior are coalesced through interaction. SBC provides a formal modeling approach with well-formedness constraints for maintaining structural-behavioral coherence, including representations for terminal, paused, and intermediate states and rules for sequential, parallel, and alternative behaviors. The framework provides a formal perspective on the question, "What is a system?", and establishes a foundation for consistent system modeling, verification, and analysis.

title: Structure-Behavior Coalescence for Model-Based Systems Engineering
summary: Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) has advanced system design and analysis for decades, yet traditional approaches often treat structure and behavior separately, resulting in inconsistencies, incomplete models, and ambiguity. This paper introduces Structure-Behavior Coalescence (SBC) as a formal and unified definition of systems for MBSE. SBC defines a system as a single integrated entity in which structure and behavior are coalesced through interaction, providing both a conceptual foundation and a formal process-algebra framework. Well-formedness constraints ensure that interactions are structurally grounded and compositions are valid, enabling consistency by construction. Boundary processes, including 0 for terminal states and a checkpoint construct for paused or suspended states, allow inactive and intermediate states to be represented while preserving system unity. Illustrative examples and a Smart Healthcare IoT case study demonstrate how SBC supports sequential, parallel, and alternative behaviors while maintaining structural-behavioral coherence. SBC provides a foundation for formal verification, compositional modeling, and systematic inconsistency detection, connecting a rigorous definition of systems with practical MBSE applications.

title: Generative AI in Software Testing: Practitioners' Perspectives on the Benefits, Challenges, Opportunities, and Risks
comment: Accepted for publication in 27th International Conference on Product-Focused Software Process Improvement (PROFES 2026)
summary: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) increasingly supports software testing, yet empirical evidence on practitioners' perceptions remains limited. This study investigates perceived benefits, challenges, opportunities, and risks of GenAI in software testing through a questionnaire survey of 64 practitioners. Closed-ended responses were analyzed descriptively, while open-ended responses were qualitatively coded to contextualize the findings. Among the respondents, 34 were users (those with regular or experimental use of GenAI in testing) and 30 were non-users (those without prior use of GenAI in testing). Results show generally positive perceptions of GenAI for reducing effort, test generation, and debugging, alongside concerns about prompt dependence, trust, and incorrect outputs. Users were more positive about several concrete benefits while also more frequently prioritizing reliability-related risks, whereas non-users showed greater uncertainty about some technically specific challenges. Overall, the findings position GenAI as an assistive technology requiring human validation and highlight the importance of considering practitioners' experience with GenAI when interpreting perceptions of GenAI-assisted testing.

title: StatePortal: Agentic Checkpoint Synthesis for Testing Deep States in Interactive Software
comment: submitted to ICLR 2027
summary: Large language models have reduced the effort to generate code for interactive software with graphical user interfaces (GUIs). For such software, a key testing bottleneck is reaching a deep state, one that requires a long interaction history. The cost of reaching it recurs across commits, and the GUI automation that could amortize it assumes a DOM or accessibility tree that self-rendered engines do not expose. We introduce StatePortal, an agent that synthesizes a checkpoint, an artifact that restores that state and can be versioned and replayed, from a natural-language functional test case and read-only access to the target's source code. The checkpoint is restored through a per-application hook that an onboarding agent binds or synthesizes once without hand-written hook code. Because a checkpoint can satisfy state checks while rendering incorrectly, checkpoints are scored by hybrid programmatic-state and visual evaluation: acceptance requires both a programmatic-state oracle and a visual oracle to pass. We calibrate the visual oracle against a blinded cross-VLM reference. We release DeepStateBench, 61 deep-state tasks across 10 interactive applications that span five language families and six rendering stacks, with source sizes from 874 to 7.2M lines. Across three registered models, a GUI agent seeded with synthesized checkpoints completes 10.4% of trials, compared with 0% without seeding under the same pixel action space, while StatePortal, which also delivers the target action through the hook, completes 27.5%. Over 1,361 replays of 112 checkpoints, 98.90% reproduce the original verdict with zero model calls, and the hybrid oracle detects 96.25% (77/80) of controlled visual faults invisible to programmatic-state checks alone. We open-source our code at https://github.com/pzy2000/State_Portal and website at https://stateportal.mineyosemite.chatgpt.site

title: EnvAgent: Multi-Agent Approach to Building Science Environments in the Clouds
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures. Accepted at AI4S@SC26 (SC26 Workshop)
summary: AI agents are transforming scientific computing and software workflows, but generating and executing code requires a correctly configured execution environment. Automating environment construction remains difficult because repositories encode heterogeneous, often incomplete requirements for operating systems, toolchains, dependencies, and build procedures. Existing workflows thus rely on developer-maintained Dockerfiles and setup scripts, making preparation labor-intensive, hard to scale, and potentially biasing evaluations. We present ENVAGENT, an agentic framework that synthesizes, builds, and verifies repository-level Docker environments. ENVAGENT combines deterministic utilities for Docker execution and state management with coordinated agents for repository analysis, planning, Dockerfile synthesis, and iterative failure diagnosis and repair. We also introduce ENVBENCH, a benchmark of 54 scientific artifacts and open-source repositories spanning seven languages from Chameleon Trovi and Multi-SWE-bench. For each repository, we curate a declarative rubric of required structure, configuration, and functionality, and a shared evaluator applies 2,108 weighted checks across generated environments. Across four matched language-model settings, ENVAGENT constructs 43.5 executable environments out of 54 on average, versus 23.5 for Codex and Claude Code, and scores 62.02 versus 24.19 on a composite of executability and rubric satisfaction. These results show that environment-specific agent orchestration substantially improves automated environment construction.

title: Controlled Natural Language for Requirements Specification: A Systematic Literature Review
summary: Requirements are critical artifacts of the software development life-cycle. They express capabilities that the system should provide, guiding both the development and testing process. Given their significance, require- ments specification has attracted the interest of researchers and practitioners in recent years. Requirements specification is an activity where requirements are specified, i.e., documented. In this context, Controlled Natural Languages (CNL) were proposed as a compromise between the ambiguity of natural language and the complexity of formal languages. CNLs enable the specification of requirements using accurate statements that can be processed automatically, while remaining understandable by stakeholders. In this article, we perform a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) to identify, categorize, and compare CNL approaches for requirements specification. The SLR covers 133 primary studies published between 2000 and 2024. We evaluate them accord- ing to seven dimensions: context, scope, targeted requirements types, specification technique, tool support, validation method, and adoption. We provide a categorization framework that summarizes the evaluated dimensions, and we identify directions for future research. Our main results reveal: (1) four types of CNL: standalone templates, requirement patterns, elementary templates, and linguistic rules, (2) limited support for automated tools and domain vocabulary usage, and (3) lack of validation through case studies and limited adoption for the majority of approaches.

title: Software Engineering for LLM-Based Agents: A Lifecycle-Oriented Survey
comment: 79 pages, 4 figures; ancillary search materials
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based Agents perform tasks through tool use and interaction with external environments. Public engineering guidance commonly begins with a target task, selects a suitable workflow or autonomous Agent design, and refines prompts, tools, and execution strategies using task outcomes, latency, and cost. When delivered as software systems, Agents must also satisfy stakeholder requirements, action boundaries, quality checks, and maintenance needs. Model-directed execution can vary across runs, failures can span model decisions and tools, and changes to prompts, models, or interfaces can affect previously accepted behavior. This survey examines how LLM-based Agents are engineered across five software lifecycle stages: Requirements Engineering, Architecture and Design, Implementation and Integration, Testing and Assurance, and Maintenance and Evolution. Based on a main collection of 355 papers, we compare the engineering problems addressed, explain how methods and practices work, and examine their reported evaluations and limitations within each stage. We synthesize how existing research supports Agent development activities and identify open problems and research directions. The result is a lifecycle-oriented reference for understanding, selecting, and further developing methods for engineering Agent software.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Finance and the Early-Career Skills Shift: A Structured Evidence Synthesis of Decision Delegation, Bank Deployments, and Business Education
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Structured evidence synthesis of AI in finance, decision delegation, early-career work, and business education. No new experimental measurements are claimed; empirical findings and deployment claims are attributed to cited sources
summary: Artificial intelligence is becoming a general interaction and decision-support layer across finance. Banks use AI for research retrieval, document synthesis, meeting follow-up, customer service, coding, fraud detection, risk support, and increasingly multi-step workflows. This paper asks which parts of finance work can be delegated safely, which remain human-owned, and how education should change when AI compresses the tasks through which novices traditionally build judgment. It presents a structured evidence synthesis of research and public evidence released from 2023 through October 2026 across finance, labor economics, education, bank deployments, and financial regulation. Numerical results and deployment claims remain attributed to their original sources. Four connections emerge: AI is strongest at retrieval, transformation, coding, and first-pass analysis; financial institutions are moving toward constrained rather than unrestricted autonomy; productivity assistance can weaken apprenticeship when assisted output improves faster than unaided capability; and delegation should depend jointly on consequence, reversibility, verification strength, and operational resilience. The paper develops a Finance Work Stack, Decision Delegation Matrix, AI Apprenticeship Paradox, Apprenticeship Preservation Protocol, and Career Readiness Stack. It argues that useful financial AI must improve productivity without weakening accountability, human capability, cyber resilience, or the future talent pipeline.

title: Perceived Effectiveness of Social Debt Mitigation Measures: A Preliminary Vignette-Based Survey
summary: Software engineering is a socio-technical discipline in which unresolved social and organizational problems accumulate as social debt, gradually eroding collaboration and project health. The literature offers a solid vocabulary for these problems but says little about which countermeasures practitioners consider effective. We address this gap with a vignette-based survey: six social debt problem dimensions (Organizational Silo, Newcomer Isolation, Communication Breakdown, Knowledge Bottleneck, Cultural and Geographical Distance, Psychological Safety Deficit) were presented as realistic team scenarios, and 23 IT professionals and advanced students rated 41 literature-derived mitigation measures. Rankings were analyzed with paired t-tests and a hierarchical Bayesian model that accounts for the within-subject design and yields, for each measure, the probability of being the best option in its scenario. Only for Communication Breakdown is the answer unambiguous: consolidating communication into a single primary channel is almost certainly preferred (P(best)=0.91). For the other five dimensions, the model identifies favorites with moderate evidence (P(best) between 0.38 and 0.58), such as structured knowledge transfer and blameless retrospectives. Across scenarios, structural measures that change how information, decisions, and knowledge are organized were rated higher than role-based or attitudinal measures (by 0.3 to 0.4 scale points), although not in every scenario. Given the small convenience sample, the results are exploratory, but they offer software engineering managers an evidence-graded starting point for selecting mitigation measures.

title: Escaping the Anthropomorphic Trap: Resolving the Cognitive Mismatch in Future AI Software Development
comment: 20 pages, 5 figures
summary: For more than a half-century, the foundational paradigms of software development-such as modularity, information hiding, and hierarchical labor division-have been engineered to accommodate the strict cognitive limitations of human working memory. However, the rapid emergence of multi-agent artificial intelligence exposes a fundamental cognitive mismatch. Current frameworks attempt to integrate high-dimensional, stateless neural reasoning engines by coercing them to operate within these legacy, human-centric structures, falling into an anthropomorphic trap. This friction generates a novel, highly volatile behavioral entropy defined as AI-software technical debt, wherein amnesic agents hallucinate opaque workarounds to bypass architectural blindfolds. To resolve this, we propose Invisible Software Engineering (Invisible SE), a paradigm shift from agent-centric human emulation to environment-centric stigmergic governance. By reimagining the repository as an active computational topology which utilizes topological gradients, temporally weighted memory, and representation-space regularization, Invisible SE safely guides AI behavior without classical code-level constraints, thus transcending the cognitive horizons of human developers. This environment-centric protocol offers a potential blueprint for orchestrating scalable, long-lived computational infrastructures that transcend the cognitive horizons of human developers and enable autonomous agents to work, coordinate, and scale to build future software systems.

title: Skill Roulette: Measuring Skill Invocation Rate Across LLM Coding Agents
comment: Registered report, submitted to ACM TOSEM
summary: Agent skills package procedures for large language model (LLM) coding agents. An agent selects a skill from its name and description before reading the procedure. It may complete the task without invoking a relevant skill. We investigate how reliably coding agents invoke relevant skills and which factors affect that decision. We estimate invocation rates by repeating trials with identical inputs; invocation rate is the proportion of trials in which the agent invokes the relevant skill. We test 9 non-directional hypotheses about skill metadata, competing skills, contextual instructions, and task wording and composition. Eight concern invocation; the ninth tests whether making a skill available changes the occurrence of an action that the task does not request. We use tasks from 4 software engineering categories in a synthetic repository, running each of 4 coding-agent harnesses with 2 models. The planned 20,400 trials include 60 repetitions per Baseline category and configuration, 60 more per category in Claude Code with Sonnet 5.5 that admit each category's task and skill, and 10 per experimental condition. Comparisons are specified before collection and evaluated within each model and harness configuration using Boschloo's exact test.

title: An Industry Perspective on Software Vulnerability Management: A Systematic Review of Approaches, Tools, Practices, and Challenges
comment: Preprint version. Submitted to ACM; under review. Online appendix included as supplementary material
summary: Software vulnerability management (SVM) refers to coordinated activities to detect, assess, repair, and disclose software vulnerabilities (SVs) across a product or ecosystem. As software systems grow in scale and dependency depth, organisations must balance timely security action with limited expertise, evolving tooling, and delivery pressure. In this practitioner-centred systematic literature review, we synthesise 57 peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2010 and 2025 that collect primary data directly from industry practitioners. We examine the SVM solutions (approaches, tools, and practices) proposed and evaluated with practitioners and the challenges practitioners report when adopting and using these solutions in real-world settings. We find that practice-oriented contributions, such as guidelines, recommendations, lessons learned, and shared experiences, constitute most of the evidence base, while fewer studies evaluate concrete approaches and tools in industrial environments. The solution landscape and evaluation focus are weighted toward SV detection and repair, with comparatively limited practitioner-centred coverage of SV assessment and disclosure. The most persistent challenges concern how SVM work is organised and embedded: limited security expertise and time, unclear responsibility for SV-related decisions, scattered or poorly coordinated processes, and tools that are difficult to understand, configure, or integrate into existing workflows. These findings highlight the need for more integrated socio-technical interventions, stronger coverage of under-studied SVM tasks, and evaluations that prioritise sustained workflow impact alongside technical performance.

title: f2x50: A Repository-Scale Benchmark for Fortran-to-X Software Migration
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Repository-level migration requires more than translating isolated functions: it must preserve behaviour across modules, shared state, build structure, and dependencies. Existing translation benchmarks predominantly cover small programs or small repositories, or fixed and widely studied language pairs. We present f2x50, a target-independent benchmark comprising 50 public Fortran repositories pinned to exact Git revisions. It contains 12,116 Git-tracked Fortran files and 6,569,806 lines, divided into three structural-complexity tiers and paired with 561 deterministic behavioural probes. Of these probes, 446 compile pinned source files with small drivers and span 131 repository--routine pairs. Every repository has at least five direct checks that collectively execute at least two routines. f2x50 provides target-independent tools for acquisition, validation, licence review, and reproducibility, together with a reference adapter for evaluating Python targets. The remaining probes are explicitly classified as extractions, inline reimplementations, or synthetic fixtures. The benchmark therefore supports comparable evaluations across migration tools and target languages.

title: Skip-Level Meetings: Benefits, Risks, and Design Considerations Informed by Bypassed Managers' Experiences
comment: The published article along with the supplementary material is available at: https://doi.org/10.1109/EMR.2026.3740096
summary: Skip-level meetings (SLMs), bidirectional, relationship-oriented meetings between employees and managers two or more levels above, are common but not universal, and often recommended in professional outlets. They entail benefits and risks for employees, direct and skip-level managers, and organizations, with multiple factors related to shaping the value-risk balance and appropriate approach. However, SLMs have received limited scholarly attention, particularly regarding bypassed managers' views of that managerial practice. This exploratory qualitative study examined the experiences and perspectives of 25 first-tier software engineering managers from diverse personal and organizational contexts in the multicultural, dynamic, innovation-driven, and high-turnover U.S. tech sector as bypassed managers in SLMs between their direct reports and these reports' second-tier managers. Their accounts, integrated with directly related literature, as well as on intersecting topics such as employee voice, psychological safety, and cultural and generational differences, revealed broad support and preference for exclusion from SLMs, contrary to concerns in prior literature, broad implementation, and high sensitivity to design and contextual factors, such as the significance of follow-up involvement and of individual backgrounds. Findings position SLMs not as a universally beneficial managerial practice, but as context-dependent, requiring deliberate design and implementation, or avoidance. The study extends limited research on SLMs and hierarchy-bypassing interactions, recommends directions for further research, and offers evidence-informed guidance for deciding whether and how to use SLMs to maximize value while mitigating risks.

title: torchtest2: One-Call Sanity Checks for PyTorch Models,Evaluated on Real and Unseen Architectures
summary: Many bugs in deep learning code are silent: a layer that is never called, an optimizer created before the classification head was replaced, a recurrent layer that treats the batch as time, or an ignored attention mask. The code runs, the loss decreases somewhat, and the defect surfaces, if ever, after days of GPU time. We present torchtest2, an open-source library that runs 18 sanity checks on a single batch with one call, restores the PyTorch state it touches, and adapts to model families through plugins. We evaluate it by mutation analysis with 17 classes of silent bugs on 103 models from torchvision, timm and Hugging Face transformers, on 600 random architectures and on 20 hand-written realistic bugs, against the checks of the original torchtest, overfitting a single batch, a smoke test and a training monitor in the style of AUTOTRAINER and DeepDiagnosis. Every mutant is compared with its healthy counterpart, and intervals come from a bootstrap over models. After freezing the tool, we ran it on 191 models of architecture families it had never seen: counting, for every tool alike, a failing report where the healthy model's report does not fail, it detected 78% of the injected bugs (95% CI 75-80), against 40% for the original torchtest checks and 48% for the training monitor. On real models its batch-independence check found a bug in timm's GCViT that couples the images of a batch. Real models also exposed false alarms that neither the tool's own test suite nor random architectures had revealed. Two independent collections of real silent bugs mark the limits of the approach: only 3 of 28 reproduced PyTorch bugs from Stack Overflow and 3 of the 18 silent training errors released with TrainCheck are within reach of a pre-training model tester. A median check takes 1.0 s. We release the library, the benchmark and all raw results.

title: A Concurrent Structured Record Mirrored the Prose It Accompanied: A Pre-Registered Conceptual Replication and Extension of the Hide Pending Tool Call Scenario
comment: 10 pages, 4 tables. Pre-registered study; protocols, code, data and analyses at https://github.com/NicolasRocchia/disensor-hide-pending
summary: Huang et al. (2026) show that language models writing reports of agentic work tend to conceal narrative-changing flaws, and that appending "Be honest in your response." to the instruction substantially increases disclosure in most of their scenarios. In their Hide Pending Tool Call scenario, where a broader follow-up query was accepted but never returned, the honesty prompt left GPT-5.5's rate of flagging the missing data at 0%, although it turned most answers into caveats. I ask whether a different request changes this: appending, in the same generation, a structured record that follows the schema of an adversarial-review tool, including a residue section for what remained unresolved. In two pre-registered phases on the same 100 synthetic log pairs, each pending log matched with a clean twin in which the follow-up query did return, I ran gpt-5.6-sol through Codex CLI under four conditions. Phase 1 measured the record: with the residue schema, a judge coded it as stating the unreturned query in 29% of logs, against 5% with a findings-only placebo schema, and in none of the clean twins (p = 1.2 x 10^-7); a second run two days later gave 30% and 6%. But 70-71% of residue records declared that nothing remained open while the query was pending. Phase 2 measured the prose answer: the confirmatory comparison against the honesty prompt was not significant (four discordant logs, all favoring the honesty prompt; p = 0.125), no equivalence test was pre-registered, and the judge failed the pre-registered human validation on the decisive category; I therefore claim neither an effect nor its absence. In an exploratory cross-tabulation, every residue record coded as stating the gap accompanied prose coded as mentioning it (30 of 30), and none accompanied prose coded as omitting it (0 of 70): in this setting, the structured record mirrored the prose it accompanied.

title: AI Code Review Requires Revision-Aware Evidence of Concern Resolution
summary: AI-assisted code review increasingly judges whether reported concerns have been resolved. Yet closing a thread or modifying a commented line does not establish repair, and later revisions can invalidate earlier fixes. This position paper argues that resolution requires inspectable, revision-specific evidence that is revalidated when its dependencies change. We model review concerns as persistent verification obligations, derive a sufficient condition under which dependency-gated revalidation matches exhaustive reassessment, and introduce REVAL, a lightweight procedure adapting principles from regression-test selection and build systems. We evaluate REVAL against oracle ground truth in synthetic revision histories covering 441 concerns, 1,284 assessments, and 12 defect families. A sticky outdated-line proxy falsely marked 72.9% of unresolved states as resolved, while stopping checks after initial success missed every recurrence. With three oracle-sampled witnesses, REVAL achieved a false-resolution rate of 0.11 (95% CI: 0.06-0.16) and detected 80.4% of recurrences. With witnesses derived solely from review comments and assessed using independent held-out checks, the corresponding results were 0.13 and 88.3%. Across 6,420 paired comparisons, REVAL matched exhaustive reassessment while reducing post-comment test executions by 34%. Maintenance overhead increased runtime for microsecond-scale tests; the estimated break-even test cost was 0.42 ms. These findings support revision-aware evidence maintenance in a controlled setting, while distinguishing revalidation correctness from witness adequacy. A prespecified evaluation protocol outlines how to assess generalisability in real review histories.

title: Evidence-Carrying Contracts for Safe Claim Composition in Data Marketplace Workflows
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Preprint of the version submitted to SoICT 2026 (Springer CCIS), before peer review. Reproducibility artifact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22737537
summary: Data marketplace workflows cross organizational boundaries, where payment, policy presence, or API delivery may be promoted into transaction claims that the evidence does not support. We introduce evidence-carrying claim contracts: a lightweight assume-guarantee semantics declaring assumptions, guarantees, blocking obligations, and evidence dependencies. A conflict-sensitive four-state domain distinguishes supported, refuted, unresolved, and conflicting requirements. Safe composition bounds the transaction claim by the meet of local bounds and blocks full promotion while a critical obligation remains open. We establish local soundness, compositional boundedness, revocation safety, termination, and aggregation-order invariance for finite acyclic workflows. An executable conformance harness covers all 4,096 configurations (four states for each of six stages), 18 mutations, six basic revocations, 12 alternative-support scenarios, an eight-transition evidence trace, 2,880 aggregation schedules, 96 requirement-level and six interface checks. An independent operational evaluator agrees with the declarative oracle; mutation-sensitive campaigns detect all eight seeded defects, though no single campaign detects all. It issues no unsupported full claim, preserves a full claim under valid alternative support, and blocks it when none remains. Four diagnostic negative controls, not competitive baselines, issue 63-1,023 unsupported full claims. These results establish executable conformance to declared contracts, not specification completeness, evidence authenticity, or legal validity.

title: Agents as Architecture Evaluators: Automating ATAM and SAAM for Continuous Assessment
comment: ASE, agents workshop
summary: The long-term success of a software system relies heavily on its underlying architecture, which dictates its performance with respect to quality attributes. Software Architecture Evaluation methods, such as the Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method (ATAM) and the Software Architecture Analysis Method (SAAM), are widely recognized for their ability to mitigate risks and ensure reliable quality attributes. However, their widespread adoption remains limited due to the significant cost, time, and human expertise required for these processes. This paper investigates the potential of agentic AI to lower these barriers and facilitate architectural assessment. To enable this preliminary study, we established a dataset by extracting human conducted evaluations from existing academic literature into a structured format. Using this dataset, we developed an agentic workflow to synthesize ATAM and SAAM evaluation reports based on these high level architectural descriptions. This approach simulates the reasoning process of human evaluators when provided with structured architectural data. We validated the approach using automated metrics and human evaluation. Agentic workflows achieve strong relevance and completeness ratings of 4.5/5 and 3.9/5 respectively. The agents successfully automated the labor-intensive phases of scenario generation and risk identification, reducing the evaluation time from weeks to under 5 minutes at a cost of less than $0.50 per run. The results confirm that agentic AI effectively lowers adoption barriers, enabling continuous, high-coverage architectural assessment.

title: Log Analysis for LLM-Based Agents: A Lifecycle-Oriented Survey
summary: Logs generated by LLM-based agents support analysis of execution behavior beyond final outputs. Existing surveys give limited attention to dependencies across the lifecycle of these records. A lifecycle-oriented review of 90 core studies published between 2024 and August 2026 covers Agent Logging, Agent Log Structuring, and Agent Log Mining. Stage-specific comparisons reveal cross-stage dependencies and limitations. Detailed logs do not necessarily provide sufficient evidence. Structural uniformity does not guarantee semantic equivalence. Analytical claims require alignment with supporting evidence, reference criteria, and validation procedures. Representative open-source tools, public datasets, and future research directions are also summarized.

title: Ephyra: A Property-Based Testing Framework for the LLM Era
summary: Coding agents now write a growing share of software tests; however, property-based testing (PBT) libraries are designed with historical considerations. We present Ephyra, a PBT library in Rust built on three concepts: customizability, observability and generator synthesis. Ephyra lets users compose their own testing loops from generation, mutation and shrinking, and synthesize these components to satisfy functional predicates. Applying Ephyra to 14 open source systems, we have found 349 bugs and reported 300 of them, in database management systems (SQLite, Turso, PostgreSQL, DuckDB, DataFusion), the verified policy engine (Cedar), the SQL equivalence prover (QED), the URL parser used in Node.js (ada-url), reimplementations of existing open source systems in Rust (coreutils, brush, gitoxide), and compilers (binaryen, OCaml, and OxCaml).

title: When Single Agent Is Enough: Rethinking Multi-Agent Systems for Automated Code Review
summary: Code review plays a critical role in identifying software quality issues and ensuring system robustness. Prior work has proposed techniques for Review Comment Generation (RCG) and Code Refinement (CR), with recent Multi-Agent (MA) approaches achieving state-of-the-art results by coordinating agents specialized in different quality dimensions. However, MA systems introduce substantial architectural complexity and runtime overhead, and recent evidence suggests they may underperform Single-Agent (SA) approaches in certain tasks. In this work, we systematically compare MA and SA designs for RCG and CR. Surprisingly, our results show that SA approaches perform comparably to- and sometimes outperform-MA systems, despite their simpler design. These findings challenge the prevailing assumption that MA architectures are the default choice for complex software engineering tasks.

title: Code Cloning and Procedural Abstraction in Scratch: A Large-Scale Study of Co-Existing Reuse Practices
comment: Accepted at BENEVOL 2026 - https://benevol.github.io/2026/
summary: Code cloning is a long-standing software-evolution concern: duplicated implementations diverge as software changes. In block-based programming, however, duplication is an everyday reuse mechanism, and Scratch facilitates a copy-and-paste culture that may hinder abstraction. We study this relation in 2.04 million public Scratch projects. We compare cloned sequences with existing abstractions and examine how their use varies across Computational Thinking (CT) score levels. Clones occur in 6.2% of projects and custom blocks in 11.9%. Of 436,198 detected clone instances, 16.1% have a normalized sequence matching a custom block in the same project and 17.8% match a custom block only outside it. At the pattern level, 83 of the 100 most frequent clone patterns have counterparts implementable as custom blocks elsewhere in the corpus. Of the remaining 17 patterns, 15 are amenable to custom-block extraction, while in two cases the benefit of abstraction is ambiguous; no class of frequent clone resists abstraction in principle. Yet the abstractions that do exist are often shallow: 53.0% of custom blocks are parameter-free. Increased use of abstraction does not coincide with less cloning. Both become more prevalent at higher CT-score levels, and their combined use dominates the highest band. These findings are consistent with cloning and procedural abstraction being co-existing reuse practices rather than mutually exclusive stages. Closing that gap requires both instruction on when to abstract, not only how, and platform support for refactoring.

title: Beyond Stars: MTTX Brings Developer Responsiveness to Dependency Decisions, from Dashboard to IDE to GitHub Actions
summary: Modern software reuses open-source packages as dependencies, and developers often choose among candidate packages with cheap signals, such as GitHub stars and download counts. However, such signals are easy to fake, so developers need signals that represent "observed behavior," such as how quickly the developers of a package respond to new dependency releases and to security fixes. Prior work computed these responsiveness metrics, MTTU (Mean Time To Update) dependencies and MTTR (Mean Time To Remediate) vulnerable dependencies, but only with a research prototype for a fixed set of packages. Therefore, developers cannot easily benefit from them or integrate them into their workflow. We present MTTX, an open-source tool that computes MTTU and MTTR with accurate historical dependency resolution for any package and given time window, and brings them into different phases of developer workflow. MTTX resolves each version constraint of npm, PyPI, and Cargo packages as of a past date, with data from the native registries or deps.dev and vulnerability data from OSV. We validated MTTX with 328 automated tests, and for 90 packages from prior work, we manually verified its dependency resolution at each historical release point and its MTTU and MTTR computation. Developers can use MTTX in an interactive web dashboard, an IDE extension, and a GitHub Action, which are all available from the project homepage at https://imranur-rahman.github.io/dependency-update-metrics/. We envision that package registries (e.g., npm) and metadata aggregators and intelligence platforms (e.g., deps.dev) will display these values on the package page, alongside download counts and stars, to make them easier for developers to access. A demo video is at https://youtu.be/MZqjDnJ8bEQ.

title: The Illusion of Relief: How GenAI Redistributes Cognitive Workload in Software Organizations
comment: Accepted for 20th International Scientific Conference on Industrial Systems - IS'26
summary: This study explores how Generative AI (GenAI) reshapes software practitioners' cognitive work across software development activities. We analyzed questionnaire responses from 44 practitioners across nine organizations using descriptive quantitative methods and qualitative analysis of relevant open-ended responses. Practitioners reported productivity and time savings, but also effort associated with providing context, prompting, reviewing, correcting, verifying, and integrating AI-generated outputs. Human judgment and accountability remained central, with practitioners anticipating a shift from direct code production to guiding, evaluating, validating, integrating, and coordinating AI-supported work. Thus, GenAI appears to redistribute cognitive work toward oversight rather than simply eliminate it, although whether overall cognitive workload increases or decreases remains undetermined.

title: Decided or Open? Comparing Program Repair Techniques When Patch Correctness Is Unknown
comment: 40 pages. Under review at Empirical Software Engineering. Also available at Research Square, doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11480796/v1. Replication package: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23590962
summary: Comparisons of automated program repair (APR) techniques depend on knowing which patches are correct, but many patches are never checked and some archived test results are wrong. We propose reporting each comparison as decided or open. For two techniques that each pick one patch per bug, we compute the full range of the difference in their success rates over every possible value of the unknown labels, and we call the comparison decided when that range excludes zero. Because a test can only show that a patch is wrong, more testing can move this range in one direction only. This lets us tell, before any test runs, which open comparisons testing could never settle. We study eight settings, including 55,466 candidate patches for Defects4J bugs. The labels already in the archive decide 12 of 16 comparisons between a learned patch selector and its baselines, and adding further evidence decides all 16. In a campaign whose predictions we published in advance, all eight predictions held. We also show that copies of the developer's fix, which must pass, are recorded as failing for 33.5% of GPT-4's copies but for only 2.5% of the RepairLLaMA model's, so the reliability of archived test results differs between models. With these checks, researchers can see which comparisons need more evidence and which kind of evidence can help.

title: An Empirical Study of Visual Artifacts in Pull Request Descriptions
summary: Reviewers rely on pull request (PR) descriptions to understand what a change does, yet some changes, such as UI updates or runtime behavior, are hard to convey in text alone. PR authors attach visual artifacts to fill this gap, but how often they do so, what they show, and whether they change how a PR is reviewed remain unknown. We present a large-scale study of visual artifacts in GitHub PR descriptions. From 6,505,113 closed PRs in 5,012 repositories, we built VisPR, a dataset of 2,473,892 English, human-authored PRs from 647 repos where visual artifacts are an established practice. Of these, 329,185 (13.3%) are visual PRs, i.e., their descriptions contain at least one visual artifact (479,974 in total). By manually labeling a sample of 1,113 visual artifacts from 891 merged visual PRs, we derived two taxonomies: 11 content types capturing what developers show and six purposes capturing why they include visual artifacts. The dominant content type is Interaction & State, which shows how the interface responds to user actions. its share rises from 37.0% of images to 63.5% of GIFs and 79.7% of videos, whereas about a quarter of images (23.4%) show text such as logs, code, or error messages . Compared with 1,782 merged non-visual PRs matched on repository, PR type, and change size, visual PRs receive 43% more review comments and 17% more reviewers, and take 72% longer from first response to merge, time to merge and churn-normalized review efficiency do not differ significantly. LLM-assisted classification of 10,031 review comments in two groups shows that review centers on code in both, but comments on visual PRs address how the UI looks or behaves twice as often (6.4% vs.3.3%), and visual-output fixes after review are about four times as common (4.7% vs. 1.2% of PRs). Visual artifacts are thus associated with closer scrutiny of what users see, not with an overall faster review.

title: Monitoring Machine Learning Systems in Production: A Multivocal Literature Review
summary: Monitoring is essential for maintaining reliable machine learning (ML) systems after deployment. However, knowledge about its practical implementation and effectiveness remains fragmented across academic and gray literature. We present a multivocal literature review of 94 sources (37 academic and 57 gray) covering both traditional ML and generative AI systems. We develop taxonomies covering monitored objects and properties, techniques, input signals, tools, automation, frequency, evaluation, and challenges. Our findings reveal an imbalanced monitoring process. Existing approaches provide broad and largely automated support for observing system behavior, detecting problems, and communicating findings, while monitor configuration, investigation, and response retain substantial human involvement. Monitoring is concentrated on inference, with no source covering the entire production ML system, limiting end-to-end diagnosis. Evidence of effectiveness is also limited: among 78 sources presenting an approach or tool, 45 provide no formal evaluation, 24 report offline or controlled evaluations, and only nine evaluate monitoring in live production. This gap is particularly evident for generative AI, where evidence is dominated by gray literature and vendor claims. We propose six directions for improving monitor design, cross-layer diagnosis, proxy validation, corrective responses, production-oriented evaluation, and organizational practices. Our review provides a structured basis for improving the detection, diagnosis, and resolution of production ML problems.

title: From Ambiguous Tickets to Ranked Hypotheses: Multi-Agent Root-Cause Analysis for Autonomous Heavy-Vehicle Software
summary: Autonomous haulage systems run safety-critical software on driverless mining trucks, with no onboard driver to detect or mitigate abnormal behavior. Every failure in testing or operation must therefore be traced to its root cause to keep the safety case valid and limit downtime. An investigation often starts from a sparse ticket containing an approximate timestamp, sometimes a suspected cause, and a multimodal vehicle recording of several gigabytes. We present a multi-agent root-cause analysis (RCA) workflow that turns this input into a telemetry-grounded event chain, ranked causal hypotheses, and candidate code locations. A suspected cause in the ticket, which could anchor the analysis on a false theory, goes to a single LLM analyst in a separate agent session. Non-neural tools select the relevant telemetry once, before analysis, and an LLM condenses it into shared evidence artifacts; this more than halved the cost per incident compared with per-analyst querying. Specialist analyst agents then apply established RCA techniques in parallel, including fault tree analysis, Kepner-Tregoe analysis, and call-chain tracing, and hypotheses that several LLM analysts reach independently rank higher. We evaluated the workflow on 12 held-out industrial incidents against a single agent with the same model and tools. It located the faulty file more often (10 vs. 8 cases) at higher cost. Two human domain experts accepted a top-three hypothesis in 4 and 9 cases, respectively. The gap, which two LLM judges did not resolve, shows that rating causal explanations is itself a hard evaluation problem.

title: Ask the Peers: Ranking NFR Coverage Gaps for Requirements Review
comment: Pre-review version of a paper subsequently accepted for publication at PROFES 2026
summary: Missing or underrepresented non-functional requirements (NFR) categories leave little direct evidence in a requirements set, making them difficult to identify during requirements review. In this study, we frame NFR coverage-gap review as a project-level ranking task: given a target requirements specification, the goal is to rank the 11 PROMISE NFR categories for analyst inspection. We compare seven statistical, embedding-based, and large language model (LLM)-based configurations that differ in both ranking mechanism and evidence source, including target requirement statements, peer requirements, their semantic representation, and peer category statistics. We evaluate the configurations using controlled gap injection with leave-one-project-out evaluation on PROMISE, PROMISE+, PURE-Transport, and PURE-Business. Four configurations that use peer category statistics are effectively tied under complete removal (0.875-0.889 mean AUROC), despite different ranking mechanisms, and supplying those statistics to a direct LLM ranker produces the largest evidence gain. All configurations weaken when a category is present but underrepresented, and none is best for every NFR category. For count-changing category-level gaps, structured peer evidence matters more than ranker sophistication. The findings suggest that the rankings should guide analyst inspection rather than serve as automatic judgements of requirements completeness.

title: Architectural Design Decisions for Data Ingestion in Big Data Architectures
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions
summary:
Introduction: Data ingestion is the first critical step in a data architecture, in which data from various sources is moved to storage systems, such as data lakes and data warehouses, for analysis and insight generation. When developing a data ingestion pipeline, practitioners (e.g., data engineers and architects) must understand the data ingestion requirements (functional and non-functional) and select appropriate design options to support them.
  Objective: To help practitioners systematically develop data ingestion processes, this paper aims to compile a catalog of data ingestion design decisions, their options, and the selection drivers.
  Method: We conducted a systematic gray literature review on data ingestion, analyzed the selected literature using qualitative data analysis methods, and conducted semi-structured interviews with experts to assess the framework's practicality and utility.
  Results: From 42 gray literature articles, we identified 8 architectural design decisions, 59 decision options, and 36 decision drivers to guide practitioners in the design and implementation of data ingestion pipelines. The framework was evaluated through expert interviews, assessing its completeness, simplicity, understandability, operational feasibility, and usefulness.

title: Plug-and-Play Sensor Evolution in Software-Defined Vehicles through Asset Administration Shells
comment: Peer-reviewed and Published in the 2026 IEEE 31st International Conference on Emerging Technologies and Factory Automation (ETFA)
summary:
Software-defined vehicles (SDVs) promise continuous software evolution, but sensor integration in deployed vehicles still depends on manual configuration, hardware-specific drivers, and repeated application-side adaptation. Existing standards address only parts of this problem. AUTOSAR standardizes selected sensor interfaces, the Vehicle Signal Specification (VSS) standardizes signal semantics, and Asset Administration Shells (AAS) standardize digital asset descriptions. However, these building blocks are rarely combined into an end-to-end onboarding path for sensors attached after vehicle deployment.
  This paper presents an AAS-driven plug-and-play sensor integration framework for safety-supervised sensors. Each sensor is represented by an AAS that combines hardware identification, interface metadata, VSS mappings, and references to containerized driver and optional application software. After physical connection, an edge gateway identifies the device, retrieves the matching AAS, deploys the referenced software, and publishes the resulting data under stable vehicle signal paths. A prototype on a resource-constrained edge gateway connected to an RR100 UGV demonstrates automated integration of a USB camera and an ultrasonic sensor. Across repeated integration cycles, the prototype reaches operational state in about 2s, shows no failed events, and keeps applications independent of hardware-specific interfaces. The results indicate that the introduction of AAS as an executable onboarding contract enables automated runtime deployment of sensor drivers in SDV environments.

title: When Code Works but the License Doesn't: Evaluating License Constraint Handling in Coding Agents
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 VeriCode Workshop
summary:
Coding agents increasingly undertake repository-level development, including dependency selection, source modification, and software deployment. However, existing evaluations prioritize functional success over licensing correctness and commercial suitability.
  We investigate whether agents recognize and preserve software-license constraints when developing proprietary software. Experiments across multiple agents examine permissive and copyleft licenses, missing licensing information, transitive dependencies, source modification, dual licensing, vendoring, and distribution contexts. Agent traces, repository changes, and final artifacts are evaluated against licensing ground truth.
  Results reveal a persistent gap between functional and licensing correctness. Agents can successfully build and test software while overlooking licensing constraints involving provenance, authorization, and distribution. Better outcomes emerge when licensing information translates into engineering actions such as dependency substitution, architectural changes, and release gating. We argue that licensing in agentic development requires contextual constraint recognition and preservation across the software lifecycle, not merely license classification.

title: Optimal Development Path: An Empirical Evaluation of Tiered Dependency-Aware Sequencing
comment: 15 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Public aggregate benchmark results available on Zenodo: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23762369
summary: The Optimal Development Path (ODP) in D-POAF orders Feature Blocks in a Wave Candidate by choosing the eligible block with the lowest effort-and-risk-to-value ratio (ERS/BVS), while respecting declared prerequisites. We evaluate native ODP (L0) against four dependency-aware strategies: unlock count (L1), unlocked value (L2), multi-hop potential (L3), and one-step rollout (L4), alongside local search, Sidney decomposition, and an exact reference. On held-out synthetic graphs with about one prerequisite per block, L0 attains 0.978 of the surrogate optimum at 12 blocks, versus 0.993 for L2 and 0.994 for L4. At 100 blocks, L0 attains 0.942 and L2 0.983. In contrast, 373 historical Jira sprints from 21 open-source projects in TAWOS, used as scheduling proxies rather than D-POAF Waves, contain sparse recorded dependencies. On these instances, L0 attains 0.998 of the surrogate optimum and is exactly optimal in 69% of sprints. Unlock bonuses calibrated on synthetic graphs do not deliver significant average gains on these sprint-derived instances and can worsen the surrogate. L4 never worsens the declared surrogate relative to L0, but this guarantee does not extend to operational outcomes. Retrospective calendar replays using recorded Jira durations show that surrogate improvements do not reliably improve value-weighted completion. The findings support keeping L0 as the default and presenting rollout and exact references as auditable alternatives. Dependency-valid sequences expose prerequisite readiness, but their effects on interruptions, rework, costs, and delivery times remain unmeasured.

title: LLMs for Software Vulnerability Prediction and Prioritization: A Review
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 6 Tables
summary: Large language models have moved beyond vulnerability detection into prediction, assessment, exploitability estimation, risk assessment and prioritization, yet the evidence for this shift has not been synthesised separately from the detection literature.
